questions.stem: A 49-year-old librarian attends the emergency department with a painful swollen right fist. She had sustained a bite injury from a stray cat 24 hours before. On examination her temperature is 38.1°C. There is an incisional wound with purulent cellulitis over the MCP joint of the ring finger on the right hand. Movement in the joint is very painful and limited. There is tracking erythema spreading up toward her elbow. Blood cultures are taken, and she is taken to theatre by the plastic surgeons for exploration and debridement of the wound. Investigations: Blood cultures Day 1: small gram-negative coccobacilli Day 2: grey mucous colonies on blood agar at 37°C. No growth on MacConkey agar
questions.lead_in: What antibiotic would be active against this organism?
questions.explanation: Penicillin The organism is most likely to be Pasteurella multocida, given the history of a penetrating cat bite, the aggressive nature of the infection manifest in the speed of onset, the associated bacteremia, and the likely tenosynovitis. The microbiology findings are consistent with this epidemiologic and clinical suspicion. Penicillin sensitivity is used within the laboratory to distinguish Pasteurella species from other gram-negative bacilli.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q36

questions.stem: A patient presents to the emergency department with a painful left hand after being bitten by a cat. He has a deep puncture wound with some purulent drainage and surrounding cellulitis. Wound cultures are taken, and he is given broad-spectrum antibiotics and tetanus vaccination.
questions.lead_in: What bacterium is the most likely cause of his infection?
questions.explanation: Pasteurella multocida Gram-negative anaerobes, including Pasteurella, are commonly associated with both cat and dog bites.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q31

questions.question: A farmer develops a lesion on his finger after being bitten by a sheep. What is the organism?
questions.question_raw: Farmer with a lesion on his finger after being bitten by a sheep
questions.model_answer: Orf virus (a Parapoxvirus). Classic occupational zoonosis of shepherds, farmers, butchers, and veterinarians with sheep/goat contact, presenting as a solitary papular-to-nodular lesion on the finger or hand; incubation ~3-7 days, self-limiting over 4-6 weeks, no specific antiviral therapy required (topical imiquimod or cidofovir tried in refractory/immunocompromised cases). Note: a true sheep bite wound can also inoculate bacterial flora, so Pasteurella multocida, streptococci, staphylococci, and anaerobes are the bacterial differential for an infected animal-bite lesion.
questions.beyond_mandell: Orf/parapoxvirus is not covered in the Mandell Pasteurella chapter; answer rests on established zoonotic dermatology (Mandell poxvirus/parapoxvirus chapter, CDC).

cohort_answer.text: Orf (caused by Parapoxvirus) - found in sheep/goats/cattle/deer, occupational exposure, incubation 3-5 days, self-limiting, no tx needed, may trial topical cidofovir or imiquimod

questions.question: [image-based question: Staphylococcus streak on blood agar plate shown with satelliting colonies] Name 3 genera of bacteria that show this satellitism characteristic.
questions.question_raw: [image-based question: Staph streak on BAP shown with satelliting colonies]

parts.text: Name 3 genera of bacteria that have this characteristic.

parts_raw.text: Name 3 genera of bacteria that have this characteristic.

questions.model_answer: (1) Haemophilus (V-factor/NAD dependent, satellites around Staphylococcus which supplies V factor from lysed erythrocytes). (2) Aggregatibacter (formerly Haemophilus/Actinobacillus spp., similar V-factor dependence). (3) Abiotrophia/Granulicatella (nutritionally variant streptococci).
questions.beyond_mandell: Abiotrophia/Granulicatella satellitism is established microbiology, not stated in this chapter.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man has a warm, erythematous, fluctuant left neck mass and is febrile. For each of the following variants, name the most likely pathogen and the MOST APPROPRIATE sample and method of diagnosis.
questions.question_raw: 24-year old with left neck fluctuant mass. It is warm, and erythematous and the patient is febrile. Name the pathogen and the MOST APPROPRIATE sample and method of diagnosis.

parts.text: Variant: he was bitten in the neck by a rabbit.
Variant: he has just immigrated from the Philippines and also describes weight loss.
Variant: he ate steak tartare 1 week prior.
Variant: he has a sore throat with exudate.

parts_raw.text: Variant: He was bit in the neck by a rabbit
Variant: He just immigrated from the Phillipines and also describes weight loss.
Variant: He ate steak tartare 1 week prior
Variant: He has a sore throat with exudate

questions.model_answer:
a) Francisella tularensis (tularemia; rabbit exposure, glandular/ulceroglandular). Diagnosis: serology (paired acute/convalescent agglutinating antibody titers) is the mainstay; if culture of a node aspirate is attempted, alert the laboratory, as F. tularensis is highly hazardous and needs special handling.
b) Mycobacterium tuberculosis (scrofula; recent immigrant from an endemic region with weight loss). Sample/method: fine-needle aspiration of the node for acid-fast smear, mycobacterial culture, and NAAT — FNA recovers M. tuberculosis in >60% of cases in high-endemic settings and is less invasive; excisional biopsy (yield up to ~90%) if FNA is non-diagnostic.
c) Toxoplasma gondii (acute toxoplasmic lymphadenitis; raw-meat ingestion). Sample/method: serology, not biopsy — seroconversion or a fourfold rise in IgG, positive IgM ELISA, or a single Sabin-Feldman dye titer >=1:1024; a negative Toxoplasma IgG essentially excludes the diagnosis.
d) Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) — suppurative cervical lymphadenitis following exudative pharyngitis/tonsillitis. Sample/method: throat swab for culture/rapid antigen plus Gram stain and culture of aspirated/drained node material; anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase B titers support the diagnosis.
questions.beyond_mandell: Tularemia diagnostic approach (serology as mainstay, laboratory biosafety alert for culture) rests on CDC/standard ID guidance; the chapter names the rabbit/tularemia association but not its specific diagnostic test.
